standard.title: Mathematical modelling
standard.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving additive and multiplicative situations including financial contexts; formulate problems using number sentences and choose calculation strategies, using digital tools where appropriate; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use mathematical modelling to solve practical additive and multiplicative problems, including money (AC9M2N06). They have not yet systematically formulated problems as number sentences for three-digit calculations, or applied modelling across both additive and multiplicative situations with explicit interpretation.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication and division in real-world and financial contexts, formulating, calculating and interpreting results.

nodes.label: Formulating problems as number sentences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can translate a practical additive or multiplicative situation into a number sentence, identifying the operation needed.
nodes.minimum_width: Translate one word problem (additive) and one word problem (multiplicative) into number sentences, identifying the operation and unknown.
nodes.typical_width: Formulate a range of practical problems as number sentences, selecting the appropriate operation; include problems with an unknown in different positions.
wider: Formulate problems involving two-step operations (e.g. buy three items, pay with $20, how much change) — bridging to multi-step modelling
Explore how the same real-world situation can be formulated differently depending on what question is asked

response_modes.reason: Students often confuse problem type when surface features change (e.g. money vs distance vs quantities). Encountering formulation across varied contexts builds the generalised skill of identifying the underlying operation.

nodes.hinge_reason: Correct problem formulation is the entry gate to the modelling cycle — students who cannot identify the operation from a practical situation cannot progress to Node 2 (strategy selection) or Node 3 (interpretation). An incorrectly formulated number sentence invalidates the entire calculation and interpretation that follows.
success_criteria: Students can write a number sentence that correctly represents a practical problem.
Students can identify which operation the problem requires and justify the choice.

nodes.label: Choosing and applying calculation strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select an appropriate calculation strategy for a given problem and apply it, including using digital tools where appropriate.
nodes.minimum_width: Solve two practical problems using different calculation strategies; for one, justify why the chosen strategy was appropriate.
nodes.typical_width: Apply a range of strategies (mental, written, digital) to practical problems; choose based on number size and context; explain strategy choice.
wider: Compare the efficiency of mental, written and digital strategies across a range of problem types, developing judgment about when each is appropriate
Investigate financial decision-making contexts where different strategies have real implications (e.g. comparison shopping)

response_modes.reason: Strategy choice requires a repertoire — students need exposure to multiple strategies across enough problem types to develop genuine selection judgment.

success_criteria: Students can select and apply a calculation strategy appropriate to the problem.
Students can identify when a digital tool is appropriate and use it to check or calculate.

nodes.label: Interpreting and communicating solutions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can interpret a calculated answer in terms of the original situation and communicate the solution with appropriate units and context.
nodes.minimum_width: Solve one practical problem and write a sentence that interprets the answer in terms of the situation (e.g. 'The total cost is $48, which means...').
nodes.typical_width: Solve and interpret a range of practical problems; communicate solutions referencing original context, including appropriate units (e.g. dollars, metres, items).
wider: Present solutions to multi-step problems with complete reasoning, including estimation check, calculation and interpretation
Explore how the same numerical answer can mean different things in different contexts (e.g. 24 apples vs $24 vs 24 minutes)

response_modes.reason: Interpretation integrates formulation, strategy and calculation into a complete modelling cycle. Students who struggle with interpretation often have a weak connection between the number sentence and the real-world situation it represents.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Multi-step problem presentation and the insight that numbers always carry contextual meaning are genuinely enriching ideas that prepare students for more complex modelling at upper primary.
success_criteria: Students can explain what their calculated answer means in terms of the original situation.
Students communicate solutions with appropriate labels and in sentences connected to the problem context.
